questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: solving for an unknown constant k from a given gradient value at a point.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of equating derivative to a given gradient value to find a parameter.

hints: Differentiate $y = 2x^2 + kx - 5$ with respect to $x$ to get $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 4x + k$.
Substitute $x = 3$ and equate the derivative to the given gradient $11$: $4(3) + k = 11$.
Solve for $k$: $12 + k = 11 \implies k = -1$.

walkthrough.text:
Differentiate the curve equation with respect to $x$:
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = 4x + k$$

Set the derivative equal to $11$ at $x = 3$:
$$4(3) + k = 11 \implies 12 + k = 11$$

ai_rubric.observable: Differentiates to obtain $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 4x + k$ and sets $4(3) + k = 11$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: solving for an unknown constant k using a stationary point condition.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of solving dy/dx = 0 to recover unknown constant.

hints: Differentiate $y = x^3 - kx^2 + 12x + 1$ to get $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 3x^2 - 2kx + 12$.
A stationary point occurs when $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$. At $x = 2$: $3(2)^2 - 2k(2) + 12 = 0$.
Simplify and solve: $12 - 4k + 12 = 0 \implies 24 = 4k \implies k = 6$.

walkthrough.text:
Differentiate the curve to find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$:
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = 3x^2 - 2kx + 12$$

Set the derivative equal to zero at $x = 2$:
$$3(2)^2 - 2k(2) + 12 = 0 \implies 12 - 4k + 12 = 0$$

Solve for $k$:
$$24 - 4k = 0 \implies 4k = 24 \implies k = 6$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: recovering a curve equation from a linear derivative and a coordinate point.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of integrating a gradient function to find curve equation.

hints: Integrate the gradient function $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 6x - 4$ to obtain $y = 3x^2 - 4x + c$.
Substitute the coordinate $(2, 7)$ into the integrated equation: $7 = 3(2)^2 - 4(2) + c$.
Solve for $c$: $7 = 12 - 8 + c \implies 7 = 4 + c \implies c = 3$. State $y = 3x^2 - 4x + 3$.

walkthrough.text:
Integrate the derivative $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 6x - 4$ to find the general curve equation:
$$y = \int (6x - 4)\,dx = 3x^2 - 4x + c$$

Substitute the point $(2, 7)$ into the equation to find the integration constant $c$:
$$7 = 3(2)^2 - 4(2) + c \implies 7 = 3(4) - 8 + c \implies 7 = 4 + c \implies c = 3$$

Write the finalized curve equation:
$$y = 3x^2 - 4x + 3$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: finding a parameter in a rational function from stationary point location.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of solving for parameters in reciprocal stationary conditions.

hints: Rewrite $y = 4x + ax^{-1}$ and differentiate: $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 4 - ax^{-2} = 4 - \dfrac{a}{x^2}$.
At $x = 3$, set $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$: $4 - \dfrac{a}{3^2} = 0 \implies 4 - \dfrac{a}{9} = 0$.
Solve for $a$: $\dfrac{a}{9} = 4 \implies a = 36$.

walkthrough.text:
Rewrite the curve equation in index form and differentiate:
$$y = 4x + ax^{-1} \implies \frac{dy}{dx} = 4 - ax^{-2} = 4 - \frac{a}{x^2}$$

Set the derivative equal to zero at the stationary point $x = 3$:
$$4 - \frac{a}{3^2} = 0 \implies 4 - \frac{a}{9} = 0$$

Solve for $a$:
$$\frac{a}{9} = 4 \implies a = 36$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: recovering a curve with reciprocal power term from its derivative.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of integrating powers including negative powers to recover curve equations.

hints: Rewrite $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 3x^2 + 4x^{-2}$ and integrate: $y = x^3 - 4x^{-1} + c = x^3 - \dfrac{4}{x} + c$.
Substitute $(1, 6)$: $6 = (1)^3 - \dfrac{4}{1} + c \implies 6 = 1 - 4 + c \implies 6 = -3 + c$.
Solve for $c$: $c = 9$. State $y = x^3 - \dfrac{4}{x} + 9$.

walkthrough.text:
Rewrite the derivative using power form and integrate with respect to $x$:
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = 3x^2 + 4x^{-2} \implies y = \int (3x^2 + 4x^{-2})\,dx = x^3 - \frac{4}{x} + c$$

Substitute the point $(1, 6)$ into the integrated expression to find $c$:
$$6 = (1)^3 - \frac{4}{1} + c \implies 6 = 1 - 4 + c \implies 6 = -3 + c \implies c = 9$$

Write the final curve equation:
$$y = x^3 - \frac{4}{x} + 9$$

ai_rubric.observable: Integrates to $y = x^3 - \dfrac{4}{x} + c$ and substitutes $(1, 6)$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: applying linear chain rule to find an unknown constant in a composite power curve.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of chain rule derivatives with unknown coefficients in stationary conditions.

hints: Differentiate $y = (2x - 1)^3 - kx$ using the chain rule: $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 3(2x - 1)^2(2) - k = 6(2x - 1)^2 - k$.
Solve for $k$: $6(9) - k = 0 \implies 54 - k = 0 \implies k = 54$.

walkthrough.text:
Differentiate $y = (2x - 1)^3 - kx$ using the linear chain rule:
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = 3(2x - 1)^2 \times 2 - k = 6(2x - 1)^2 - k$$

Set the derivative equal to zero at the stationary point $x = 2$:
$$6(2(2) - 1)^2 - k = 0 \implies 6(3)^2 - k = 0$$

Solve for $k$:
$$6(9) - k = 0 \implies 54 - k = 0 \implies k = 54$$

ai_rubric.observable: Differentiates to obtain $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 6(2x - 1)^2 - k$ and sets $6(3)^2 - k = 0$.

questions.difficulty_reason: One chain-rule derivative is followed by a direct stationary condition at a supplied positive coordinate.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: A stationary condition determines a constant in a square-root curve; this new curve has a different composite input, linear term, coordinate and parameter relation.

hints: Differentiate $y = p(2x+1)^{1/2} - 3x$ to obtain $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{p}{\sqrt{2x+1}} - 3$.
At $x = 4$, set $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$: $\dfrac{p}{\sqrt{2(4)+1}} - 3 = 0 \implies \dfrac{p}{3} - 3 = 0$.
Solve for $p$: $\dfrac{p}{3} = 3 \implies p = 9$.

walkthrough.text:
Differentiate $y = p(2x+1)^{1/2} - 3x$ using the linear chain rule:
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = p\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)(2x+1)^{-1/2} \times 2 - 3 = \frac{p}{\sqrt{2x+1}} - 3$$

Set $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$ at the stationary point $x = 4$:
$$\frac{p}{\sqrt{2(4)+1}} - 3 = 0 \implies \frac{p}{\sqrt{9}} - 3 = 0 \implies \frac{p}{3} = 3$$

Solve for the positive constant $p$:
$$p = 9$$

hints: Substitute $x = 1$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 6$ into the given gradient formula $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 4(2x - 1)^2 + kx$.
Evaluate: $6 = 4(2(1) - 1)^2 + k(1) \implies 6 = 4(1)^2 + k \implies 6 = 4 + k$.
Solve for $k$: $k = 6 - 4 = 2$.

walkthrough.text:
Substitute $x = 1$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 6$ into the given gradient function:
$$6 = 4(2(1) - 1)^2 + k(1)$$

Simplify the expression:

questions.difficulty_reason: A quadratic equation in a parameter must be formed from a stationary condition and solved subject to a positivity constraint.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: A stationary coordinate generates a quadratic relation in a constant; this original problem uses a new three-term gradient function.

hints: Simplify into a quadratic equation in $a$: $a^2 + 4a - 12 = 0$.
Factorise: $(a + 6)(a - 2) = 0 \implies a = -6 \text{ or } a = 2$.
Since $a$ is a positive constant, choose $a = 2$.

walkthrough.text:
Set the gradient function $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = a^2 + 2ax - 3x^2$ equal to zero at the stationary point $x = 2$:
$$a^2 + 2a(2) - 3(2)^2 = 0 \implies a^2 + 4a - 12 = 0$$

Factorise the quadratic equation in $a$:
$$(a + 6)(a - 2) = 0 \implies a = -6 \quad \text{or} \quad a = 2$$

Apply the condition that $a > 0$ to select the valid value:
$$a = 2$$

questions.difficulty_reason: A two-part question where finding a stationary parameter is immediately followed by integrating to recover the original cubic curve.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: The source finds a parameter from a stationary condition and integrates the resulting derivative; this original problem uses a different quadratic gradient.

hints: The gradient at $(1, 5)$ is zero, so set $\left.\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=1} = 0$.
Substitute $x = 1$: $3(1)^2 - k(1) + 1 = 0 \implies 3 - k + 1 = 0$.
Solve for $k$: $4 - k = 0 \implies k = 4$.

walkthrough.text:
Set the gradient function $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 3x^2 - kx + 1$ equal to zero at $(1, 5)$:
$$3(1)^2 - k(1) + 1 = 0 \implies 3 - k + 1 = 0$$

Solve for $k$:

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Integration to recover the curve follows parameter recovery.

hints: Substitute $k = 4$ into the gradient function: $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 3x^2 - 4x + 1$.
Integrate with respect to $x$: $y = x^3 - 2x^2 + x + c$.
Use the point $(1, 5)$: $5 = (1)^3 - 2(1)^2 + (1) + c \implies 5 = 1 - 2 + 1 + c \implies 5 = c$.
State the curve equation: $y = x^3 - 2x^2 + x + 5$.

walkthrough.text:
Substitute $k = 4$ into the gradient function to obtain the concrete derivative:
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = 3x^2 - 4x + 1$$

Integrate with respect to $x$ to find the general curve equation:
$$y = \int (3x^2 - 4x + 1)\,dx = x^3 - 2x^2 + x + c$$

Use the given point $(1, 5)$ to find the constant of integration $c$:
$$5 = (1)^3 - 2(1)^2 + (1) + c \implies 5 = 1 - 2 + 1 + c \implies 5 = 0 + c \implies c = 5$$

State the finalized curve equation:
$$y = x^3 - 2x^2 + x + 5$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Integrating a linear chain-rule cubic term alongside a linear term and applying a fractional y-intercept to find the constant.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: The source recovers a curve by integrating composite powers; this task integrates a cubic linear term and applies a non-integer intercept.

hints: Integrate $4(2x+1)^3$ using reverse chain rule: $\int 4(2x+1)^3\,dx = \dfrac{4(2x+1)^4}{4 \times 2} = \dfrac{1}{2}(2x+1)^4$.
Integrate $-6x$: $\int -6x\,dx = -3x^2$.
Combine with constant of integration: $y = \dfrac{1}{2}(2x+1)^4 - 3x^2 + c$.
Substitute $\left(0, \dfrac{7}{2}\right)$: $\dfrac{7}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}(1)^4 - 3(0)^2 + c \implies \dfrac{7}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} + c \implies c = 3$.

walkthrough.text:
Integrate the composite term $4(2x+1)^3$ with respect to $x$ using the reverse chain rule:
$$\int 4(2x+1)^3\,dx = \frac{4(2x+1)^4}{4 \times 2} = \frac{1}{2}(2x+1)^4$$

Integrate the $-6x$ term and add the constant of integration:
$$y = \frac{1}{2}(2x+1)^4 - 3x^2 + c$$

Substitute the given point $\left(0, \dfrac{7}{2}\right)$ to solve for $c$:
$$\frac{7}{2} = \frac{1}{2}(2(0) + 1)^4 - 3(0)^2 + c \implies \frac{7}{2} = \frac{1}{2}(1) + c \implies c = \frac{7}{2} - \frac{1}{2} = 3$$

State the final equation of the curve:
$$y = \frac{1}{2}(2x + 1)^4 - 3x^2 + 3$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Solving for two unknown coefficients requires combining tangent and normal gradient conditions at two different x-values into a 2x2 linear system.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: The source combines tangent and normal data at two distinct x-coordinates to solve for two polynomial parameters.

hints: Differentiate $y = x^3 + ax^2 + bx + 1$ to obtain $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 3x^2 + 2ax + b$.
At $x = 1$, tangent gradient is $2$: $3(1)^2 + 2a(1) + b = 2 \implies 3 + 2a + b = 2 \implies 2a + b = -1$.
At $x = 2$, normal gradient is $-\dfrac{1}{7}$, so tangent gradient is $7$: $3(2)^2 + 2a(2) + b = 7 \implies 12 + 4a + b = 7 \implies 4a + b = -5$.
Subtract equations: $(4a + b) - (2a + b) = -5 - (-1) \implies 2a = -4 \implies a = -2$.
Find $b$: $2(-2) + b = -1 \implies -4 + b = -1 \implies b = 3$. State $y = x^3 - 2x^2 + 3x + 1$.

walkthrough.text:
Differentiate the cubic curve to find the gradient function in terms of $a$ and $b$:
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = 3x^2 + 2ax + b$$

Use the tangent gradient condition at $x = 1$ ($m_T = 2$):
$$3(1)^2 + 2a(1) + b = 2 \implies 3 + 2a + b = 2 \implies 2a + b = -1 \quad \text{--- (1)}$$

Use the normal gradient at $x = 2$ ($m_N = -\dfrac{1}{7}$) to deduce the tangent gradient $m_T = 7$:
$$m_T = -\frac{1}{-1/7} = 7$$
$$3(2)^2 + 2a(2) + b = 7 \implies 12 + 4a + b = 7 \implies 4a + b = -5 \quad \text{--- (2)}$$

Solve the simultaneous equations (2) - (1):
$$(4a + b) - (2a + b) = -5 - (-1) \implies 2a = -4 \implies a = -2$$
$$2(-2) + b = -1 \implies -4 + b = -1 \implies b = 3$$

Substitute $a = -2$ and $b = 3$ to state the complete curve equation:
$$y = x^3 - 2x^2 + 3x + 1$$

ai_rubric.observable: Uses tangent gradient at $x=1$ to obtain $2a+b=-1$.
Uses normal gradient $-\dfrac{1}{7}$ to identify tangent gradient $7$ at $x=2$.
Solves simultaneous equations to obtain $a=-2$ and $b=3$.

questions.difficulty_reason: A multi-part question linking parallel-tangent gradient and curve-passage conditions to solve for two constants, then finding the tangent equation at a second point.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: The source combines a parallel tangent condition and a coordinate passage point to determine two curve parameters.

hints: Differentiate $y = x^3 + ax^2 + bx - 6$ to get $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 3x^2 + 2ax + b$.
The tangent at $x = 1$ is parallel to $y = 4x - 5$ ($m = 4$): $3(1)^2 + 2a(1) + b = 4 \implies 2a + b = 1$.
Substitute $(3, 18)$ into the curve: $18 = (3)^3 + a(3)^2 + b(3) - 6 \implies 18 = 27 + 9a + 3b - 6 \implies 9a + 3b = -3 \implies 3a + b = -1$.
Solve the system: $(3a + b) - (2a + b) = -1 - 1 \implies a = -2$. Then $2(-2) + b = 1 \implies b = 5$.

walkthrough.text:
Differentiate the curve to find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$:
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = 3x^2 + 2ax + b$$

The tangent at $x = 1$ is parallel to $y = 4x - 5$, so its gradient is $4$:
$$3(1)^2 + 2a(1) + b = 4 \implies 3 + 2a + b = 4 \implies 2a + b = 1 \quad \text{--- (1)}$$

Use the fact that the curve passes through $(3, 18)$:
$$18 = (3)^3 + a(3)^2 + b(3) - 6$$
$$18 = 27 + 9a + 3b - 6 \implies 9a + 3b = -3 \implies 3a + b = -1 \quad \text{--- (2)}$$

Subtract equation (1) from equation (2) to solve for $a$ and $b$:
$$(3a + b) - (2a + b) = -1 - 1 \implies a = -2$$
$$2(-2) + b = 1 \implies -4 + b = 1 \implies b = 5$$

ai_rubric.observable: Uses parallel tangent condition at $x=1$ to obtain $2a+b=1$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Finding the tangent equation after recovering the underlying curve constants.

hints: With $a = -2$ and $b = 5$, the curve is $y = x^3 - 2x^2 + 5x - 6$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 3x^2 - 4x + 5$.
Evaluate the gradient at $x = 2$: $m = 3(2)^2 - 4(2) + 5 = 12 - 8 + 5 = 9$.
Evaluate the point on the curve at $x = 2$: $y = (2)^3 - 2(2)^2 + 5(2) - 6 = 8 - 8 + 10 - 6 = 4 \implies (2, 4)$.
Write the tangent equation: $y - 4 = 9(x - 2) \implies y = 9x - 18 + 4 \implies y = 9x - 14$.

walkthrough.text:
Substitute $a = -2$ and $b = 5$ into the gradient function:
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = 3x^2 - 4x + 5$$

Calculate the tangent gradient at $x = 2$:
$$m = \left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=2} = 3(2)^2 - 4(2) + 5 = 12 - 8 + 5 = 9$$

Calculate the corresponding $y$-coordinate on the curve $y = x^3 - 2x^2 + 5x - 6$ at $x = 2$:
$$y = (2)^3 - 2(2)^2 + 5(2) - 6 = 8 - 8 + 10 - 6 = 4 \implies (2, 4)$$

Construct the equation of the tangent line through $(2, 4)$ with slope $m = 9$:
$$y - 4 = 9(x - 2) \implies y = 9x - 18 + 4 \implies y = 9x - 14$$
